‼️DEVELOPING: RADAR SHOWS JET FLEW INTO A STORM CORE AT 35,000 FEET

Analysis of Miami NEXRAD radar shows the Learjet 60 (N722BD) entered a thunderstorm core near Wellington at about 12:48 PM ET, just before it crashed in Palm Beach County.

At 35,000 feet, radar echoes around the jet jumped to 34 dBZ, with a 52 dBZ core below it and storm tops near 47,000 feet. Tracking data shows the jet climbed about 450 feet inside the core, then went into a spiraling dive and crashed 76 seconds later.

Minutes earlier, the crew told Miami Center they were in moderate turbulence and “managing the ice” at −53°F, and asked to climb out of the precipitation. Moments later they declared a Mayday, reported an overspeed, and said they were banking 60 degrees.

All 9 people on board did not make it. The NTSB is investigating, and the cause has not been determined.

Yesterday, we went to the shelter to adopt a black cat.

Everything was set beforehand: treats, toys, excitement, all of it.

But as soon as we saw her, the scene changed.

She was not like normal cats.
Crouched in a corner, head down, completely silent.

No interest, no reaction.
The staff said, “She has been here for a long time; people ignore her.”

Because she is a black cat.

People just see her and move on.
She was sitting there as if everyone had abandoned her.

We looked at each other; no discussion took place.
It was a direct decision.
“We are taking her.”

The journey home was silent.
She was completely quiet in the carrier.
No movement, no sound.

Just closed off inside.

Sometimes she would slightly lift her head and look out the window.

Even upon reaching home, she went to a corner.

And fell asleep there.

Maybe for the first time, she felt safe.
She doesn’t trust yet; fear still exists.
But now she is not alone.

And that is the most important thing.
